title_en: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?
author: Clement of Alexandria
addressee: Christians concerned about the salvation of the wealthy, especially those who teach or counsel the rich
occasion: Clement addresses believers who take Jesus' saying about the camel and the needle's eye literally and despair of rich Christians being saved, and he also criticizes those who flatter the rich. He writes to remove false despair and show how the rich may be saved.
argument: Clement argues that Jesus' command to sell one's possessions is not a command to become outwardly poor, but to renounce the passions and attachments of the soul that wealth can excite. The rich man in the Gospel is not condemned for having wealth, but for loving it more than eternal life. Salvation depends on the soul's disposition, not on external possessions, and wealth can be used rightly for love of neighbor. Clement then shows that the greatest commandments are love of God and love of neighbor, and that the rich can fulfill them by using wealth to serve Christ in the poor. He closes by urging repentance and offering the story of the apostle John and the young robber as proof that no sinner, however fallen, is beyond hope.

outline.move: Clement criticizes flatterers of the rich and those who despair of rich Christians, and sets out his pastoral aim: to remove false despair and show how the rich may be saved.
He quotes the Gospel story of the rich man from Mark and insists that Jesus' words must be interpreted spiritually, not superficially.
He explains the rich man's question and Jesus' answer, showing that the man kept the law but still lacked the one thing needed: the gift of eternal life from Christ.
He argues that 'sell your possessions' means casting out the soul's passions and attachments to wealth, not necessarily abandoning external goods, since wealth can be used for good.
He distinguishes true spiritual poverty and riches from false outward poverty and riches, and explains why the rich man went away sad and why the disciples were alarmed.
He interprets the disciples' question and Jesus' promises about leaving family and possessions, showing that Christ calls for spiritual detachment, not hatred of family or literal destitution.
He turns to the positive path: the greatest commandments are love of God and love of neighbor, and the rich can fulfill them by using wealth to serve Christ in the needy.
He urges the rich to open their hearts to all who are enrolled as disciples of God and to acquire such godly persons as spiritual bodyguards through their wealth, without judging worthiness.
He presents the mystery of divine love, showing God as love, and then quotes Paul on love as the surpassing way of salvation.
He insists that repentance is always possible, describes true repentance as turning from sin, and urges the rich to submit to a spiritual guide.
He tells the story of the apostle John and the young robber as a proof that even the worst sinner can be restored through repentance, and closes with a doxology.

key_terms.sense: A rich person; Clement distinguishes the outwardly rich from those rich in passions and from the truly rich in virtues
A poor person; Clement distinguishes outward poverty from spiritual poverty and true poverty of passions
Wealth or riches, treated as an indifferent instrument that can be used well or badly
Money or material goods, which Clement says are not to be thrown away but used rightly
Possessions or property, especially external goods that can be used for good or ill
The passions or disordered attachments of the soul, which are the real things to be sold and renounced
Freedom from the passions, the state of soul required for salvation
Salvation, eternal life, the goal Clement says is open to the rich if rightly disposed
The kingdom of heaven, the inheritance promised to those who follow Christ
Eternal life, the gift the rich man asked for and which Christ alone gives
The commandments of God and Christ, which must be kept for salvation
Love, especially love of God and neighbor, the greatest commandment and the way of salvation
Repentance, the true turning from sin that restores the fallen
Treasure, used of both earthly and heavenly treasure, and of the good or evil treasure of the heart
Mammon of unrighteousness, worldly wealth that can be used to make friends for eternal dwellings

scripture: Clement quotes the Gospels, especially Mark, and also Matthew and Luke, along with Paul's letters, 1 John, and Old Testament prophetic texts. He uses Septuagint book names and Psalm numbering. In modern form, cite Gospel passages as Mark 10:17-31, Matthew 19:16-30, Luke 18:18-30, and Old Testament quotations according to standard English Bible book names and numbering.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is approximate; it is generally placed in the late second century.
The precise identity of the city in the story of John and the young robber is not given; Clement says 'some mention its name.'
The text of section 1 has lacunae, so some phrases are reconstructed.
The exact wording of some biblical quotations varies among manuscripts and Gospel versions.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Clement addresses believers who take Jesus' saying about the camel and the needle's eye literally and despair of rich Christians being saved, and he also criticizes those who flatter the rich.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οἱ μὲν τοὺς ἐγκωμιαστικοὺς λόγους τοῖς πλουσίοις δωροφοροῦντες... ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀσεβεῖς καὶ ἐπίβουλοι... Κινδυνεύει δὲ οὐχ ἁπλοῦν τι εἶναι τὸ αἴτιον τοῦ τὴν σωτηρίαν χαλεπωτέραν τοῖς πλουτοῦσι δοκεῖν... οἱ μὲν γὰρ αὐτόθεν καὶ προχείρως ἀκούσαντες τῆς τοῦ κυρίου φωνῆς... ἀπογνόντες ἑαυτοὺς ὡς οὐ βιωσόμενοι...
_unresolved_facts.fix: Clement addresses two distinct groups: first, those who flatter the rich with encomiastic speeches (section 1), and second, two types among the rich themselves—those who despair of salvation upon hearing Jesus' saying literally (section 2, first group), and those who understand correctly but neglect the necessary works for salvation (section 2, second group). The brief conflates these into 'believers who...despair' and 'those who flatter the rich,' but the flatterers are a separate target of criticism, not the ones who despair.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Levi... A rich tax collector mentioned alongside Zacchaeus and Matthew as wealthy persons Jesus visited.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: αὐτός τε ἐπιξενοῦται Ζακχαίῳ καὶ Λευεὶ καὶ Ματθαίῳ τοῖς πλουσίοις καὶ τελώναις
_unresolved_facts.fix: Levi is mentioned alongside Zacchaeus and Matthew, but the source does not explicitly call Levi a 'tax collector' (τελώνης) in this passage—rather, all three are described as 'rich and tax collectors' (τοῖς πλουσίοις καὶ τελώναις). However, Levi is traditionally identified with Matthew in the Gospels, so this may be a separate person or the same person mentioned twice. The brief should note this ambiguity rather than confidently identifying Levi as a separate 'rich tax collector.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: Matthew... A rich tax collector, named with Levi as an example of a wealthy person Jesus visited.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: αὐτός τε ἐπιξενοῦται Ζακχαίῳ καὶ Λευεὶ καὶ Ματθαίῳ τοῖς πλουσίοις καὶ τελώναις
_unresolved_facts.fix: Matthew is mentioned, but the source groups all three (Zacchaeus, Levi, and Matthew) together as 'rich and tax collectors.' The brief's phrasing suggests Matthew and Levi are separate examples, but biblically Levi and Matthew are the same person. The source may be listing them separately for rhetorical effect or may refer to different individuals; the brief should acknowledge this uncertainty.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The young robber... Does not speak in words; his response is shown through actions, groans, and tears
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὃ δὲ ἀκούσας πρῶτον ἔστη μὲν κάτω βλέπων. εἶτα ἔρριψε τὰ ὅπλα, εἶτα τρέμων ἔκλαιε πικρῶς· προσελθόντα δὲ τὸν γέροντα περιέλαβεν, ἀπολογούμενος ταῖς οἰμωγαῖς ὡς ἐδύνατο καὶ τοῖς δάκρυσι βαπτιζόμενος ἐκ δευτέρου. μόνην ἀποκρύπτων τὴν δεξιάν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The young robber does not speak quoted words, but he is described as 'apologizing with groans as best he could' (ἀπολογούμενος ταῖς οἰμωγαῖς ὡς ἐδύνατο), which indicates vocalized response beyond mere actions. The brief's claim 'does not speak in words' is too strong; he communicates through non-verbal vocalization (groans) rather than articulate speech.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The bishop... First described with indirect narration, then quoted directly in the closing story
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τοῦ δὲ δεχομένου καὶ πάνθ᾿ ὑπισχνουμένου... ὃ δὲ τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ἐξεπλάγη... »ἐκεῖνος« ἔφη »τέθνηκε«... »θεῷ τέθνηκεν« εἶπεν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The bishop/elder is quoted directly (ἔφη, εἶπεν), but there is no prior 'indirect narration' of his speech—only narrative description of his actions (receiving, promising, being astonished). The brief's claim of 'first described with indirect narration, then quoted directly' misrepresents the narrative structure; he is described with narrative verbs of action, not indirect speech, before being quoted directly.

_unresolved_facts.claim: A father or relative (hypothetical)... Introduced as a hypothetical speaker in a courtroom-like scene
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ μὲν πατήρ σοι δοκείτω παρεστὼς λέγων ›ἐγώ σε ἔσπειρα καὶ ἔθρεψα...‹
_unresolved_facts.fix: The hypothetical speaker is specifically 'the father' (ὁ πατήρ), not 'a father or relative.' The brief's expansion to 'or relative' is unsupported; the text specifies πατήρ, and later mentions brother, child, or wife (ἀδελφὸς... τέκνον... γυνή) as other potential obstacles, but the primary hypothetical speaker is the father.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Christ (hypothetical)... Introduced as the opposing speaker in the same hypothetical scene
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἑτέρωθεν δὲ ἄκουε τοῦ σωτῆρος· ›ἐγώ σε ἀνεγέννησα...‹
_unresolved_facts.fix: The opposing speaker is introduced as 'the Savior' (τοῦ σωτῆρος), not specifically as 'Christ.' While these are often interchangeable, the brief should note the source uses σωτήρ, not Χριστός, in this passage.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Anaxagoras... A pagan philosopher cited as one who gave up wealth for the wrong reasons; the plural form may refer to followers or the type.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source uses plural forms (Ἀναξαγόραι, Δημόκριτοι, Κράτητες), which are not standard for these philosophers. The brief's note 'the plural form may refer to followers or the type' is speculative. More likely, these are rhetorical plurals or references to multiple individuals of the same philosophical type, or possibly textual variants. The brief should acknowledge uncertainty rather than confidently identifying them as specific philosophers with a speculative explanation for the plural.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections 33-36: He urges the rich to open their hearts to all who are enrolled as disciples of God and to acquire such godly persons as spiritual bodyguards through their wealth, without judging worthiness.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πᾶσιν ἄνοιξον τὰ σπλάγχνα τοῖς τοῦ θεοῦ μαθηταῖς ἀπογεγραμμένοις... τοιούτους κτῆσαι τῷ σῷ πλούτῳ καὶ τῷ σώματι καὶ τῇ ψυχῇ δορυφόρους
_unresolved_facts.fix: The outline oversimplifies by saying 'without judging worthiness.' The text does say 'do not judge' (μὴ κρῖνε), but the rationale is specific: one might err in judgment (ἐνδέχεται γάρ σε διαμαρτεῖν περὶ τὴν δόξαν), and it's better to help the unworthy than to risk neglecting the godly. The 'without judging worthiness' framing loses the specific reasoning about the danger of misjudgment and the positive duty to help all disciples.
